chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
title: A gas stop near Shreveport and the sandwich shop
summary: After filling up in Longview and Shreveport, Fields describes his band's members and how Warren Luckey and Carl White went for sandwiches.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: While we're talking, all of those incidents and something like that happened, but while we're talking about the incidents, on the outskirts of Shreveport, Louisiana, we came out of Longview, Texas, we played Longview, Texas and on Texas Avenue, went in there to fill up with gas. I had this bus, forty gallons on each side and if you're anywhere low, that's a pretty good trick for a filling station. So I always asked them if we could use the bathroom and if any of them say we can't I drive off, and I heard some of them when I do, they would say, I don't blame you but that's the rule.

Anyway, this filling station welcomed us and everything and we filled up and while we were there a couple of the guys said, I'm going across and get a sandwich and I said okay and they went on across and we got through and had washed up, used the bathroom, filled up and everything and we were all sitting in the bus. We had two or three pistols in the bus; I used to carry my shotgun (inaudible) and Warren Luckey, I don't know if you ever knew him, a very nice musician, but he didn't spend too long a time in the band. He said he could not put up with all that stuff in the south. He was Texan but he fell in along New York and he did all right; he married a girl up in New York.

And Parker was in the band then and Luther West was in the band--I'm trying to think who else--I believe Artis Paul was in the band then. We had a big band and several good outstanding musicians there, and
Carl White--did you ever know him, a bass player?

Carl was a youngster at that time, but Warren was a football player and he was really on the ball. They went in this little joint to get a sandwich and they asked if they could get a sandwich and the man said yeah, and someone sitting around, I guess, you got no business in here, nigger, and so the proprietor said, the men want to get a sandwich to go--I think it was to go--they got no business coming in the front door. And so the man kept telling them they ain't going to be doing nothing.
